CHASE: Competing Hypotheses for Ambiguity-Aware Selective Prediction

Kartik Jhawar Affiliation: Institute for Digital Molecular Analytics and Science, NTU, Singapore 636921 Affiliation: School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, NTU, Singapore 639798    Yuhao Geng Affiliation: Institute for Digital Molecular Analytics and Science, NTU, Singapore 636921    Atul N. Parikh Affiliation: Institute for Digital Molecular Analytics and Science, NTU, Singapore 636921 Affiliation: School of Materials Science and Engineering, NTU, Singapore 639798 Affiliation: Singapore Centre for Environmental Life Sciences Engineering, NTU, Singapore 637551    Lipo Wang Email: elpwang@ntu.edu.sg*First author†Corresponding author Affiliation: Institute for Digital Molecular Analytics and Science, NTU, Singapore 636921 Affiliation: School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, NTU, Singapore 639798
Abstract

Standard selective prediction methods typically estimate uncertainty from the output of a single predictive branch. While effective for general uncertainty estimation, these approaches often struggle under partial observability, where local temporal evidence can be contradictory and standard confidence scores become misleading. We introduce CHASE (Competing Hypotheses for Ambiguity-Aware Selective Prediction), a selective prediction framework that explicitly compares structured temporal explanations to determine whether to commit to a decision or abstain. Because genuine ambiguity causes the score gap between competing hypotheses to collapse, CHASE optimizes a ranking-aware selector over these hypothesis margins to globally separate safe commitments from fundamentally uncertain ones. We evaluate this framework on the problem of hidden connectivity inference, utilizing a controlled, physically grounded simulator inspired by the dynamics of giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs), alongside zero-shot qualitative transfer (without retraining or fine tuning) to representative real GUV videos. Our experiments demonstrate that explicitly reasoning over competing hypotheses provides a superior balance of metrics. Compared to canonical uncertainty baselines, CHASE achieves statistically significant gains in overall no-abstain accuracy, three-way accuracy, and overall ambiguity-aligned abstention (at 80% coverage). Specifically, it yields up to an 11.0% relative mean improvement in overall alignment, alongside up to an 8.8% relative boost in three-way accuracy in the very-high ambiguity regime. By maintaining a selective risk boundary strictly at par with the best baselines at 80% coverage, and reducing overall risk by 9.9% at 90% coverage, this framework offers a more reliable approach to decision-making under structured ambiguity.

1 Introduction

Real-world decisions are often difficult not because signals are globally weak, but because they are locally misleading. A system may show short periods of strong agreement, short periods of disagreement, or partial visual evidence that appears and disappears over time. Because standard classifiers are forced to make confident binary decisions from this incomplete evidence, selective prediction is crucial: a model must learn to commit only when evidence is sufficient, and abstain otherwise.

Existing approaches usually estimate uncertainty from a single predictive branch, either by thresholding confidence, measuring predictive variability, or learning a reject option jointly with classification Geifman and El-Yaniv (2017); Gal and Ghahramani (2016); Lakshminarayanan et al. (2017); Geifman and El-Yaniv (2019); Liu et al. (2019); Corbière et al. (2019). This setting exposes a limitation of generic confidence-based abstention. These are strong and necessary baselines, but they still score uncertainty mainly from the output of one predictive branch. This particularly becomes limiting when the evidence is only partially observable and supports competing explanations over time. In such settings, the difficulty is not simply low confidence. The real difficulty is that short temporal segments can look convincing in different ways, and global summary cues can become misleading. A model should therefore not only ask “how confident am I?”, but also “which explanation is better supported, and is that difference reliable enough to justify commitment?”.

In this paper, we propose a simple alternative, hypothesis-driven selective prediction. Instead of using a single predictive branch, we explicitly compare two competing temporal hypotheses (e.g., connected versus disconnected dynamics) for each video sequence. The core intuition is straightforward: when evidence is clear, the correct hypothesis explains the sequence significantly better than the alternative, creating a large score gap; when evidence is ambiguous, neither hypothesis dominates, and this gap collapses. Rather than relying on a manual threshold to evaluate this margin, CHASE learns a global selector that optimally ranks these gaps. Crucially, to ensure safe decision-making, this selector is trained to explicitly penalize both prediction errors and structural ambiguity. By doing so, the acceptance score is aligned not only with binary correctness (avoiding pure errors) but also with selective decision quality (refusing to gamble on misleading evidence). The idea is generic. Whenever a sequential decision can be expressed as a small number of structured competing explanations under partial observability, direct comparison between those explanations can be more informative than a single confidence score alone (Figure 1).

We ground this framework in the problem of hidden connectivity inference from videos of giant unilamellar vesicles (GUVs). GUVs are cell-sized lipid vesicles that are often used as simplified physical models of membrane systems. Under osmotic stress, GUVs deform and can either remain tethered by a microscopic neck or separate completely. Our task is to classify this binary connectivity from 2D projections where the physical neck (bridge) can be weak, intermittent, out of plane, or invisible. This provides a natural testbed for ambiguity-aware selective prediction, because motion correlation, proximity, and bridge intensity can disagree. Although 3D reconstruction provides connectivity labels for selected examples, the available real videos do not provide a large, systematically annotated benchmark covering all ambiguity regimes. Therefore, our primary quantitative evaluation uses a controlled, physically grounded simulator, while empirical GUV sequences are used strictly for qualitative zero-shot transfer (without retraining or fine tuning).

In summary, this paper makes three contributions:

  • •

    We introduce a hypothesis-driven formulation of selective prediction for temporally ambiguous decisions under partial observability.

  • •

    We develop a physically grounded simulator for hidden connectivity inference that systematically covers the ambiguity regimes needed for controlled evaluation.

  • •

    We demonstrate that explicitly reasoning over competing hypotheses yields significant gains in ambiguity-aware metrics-specifically three-way accuracy and abstain alignment-without compromising standard selective risk, supported by qualitative zero-shot transfer to real GUV videos.

1.1 Related Work

Selective prediction and epistemic uncertainty: Early rejection frameworks (Bartlett and Wegkamp, 2008; Cortes et al., 2016) and deep selective classifiers (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Corbière et al., 2019) balance accuracy and coverage, recently refined via cost-sensitive losses and calibrated selection (Charoenphakdee et al., 2021; Narasimhan et al., 2024; Fisch et al., 2022; Galil et al., 2023). Parallel work estimates epistemic uncertainty-via ensembles, dropout, or evidential models (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017; Sensoy et al., 2018; Charpentier et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2020; Daxberger et al., 2021)-to provide downstream confidence signals. However, as formalized by Hüllermeier and Waegeman (2021), abstention should stem from actual disagreement, not just low softmax probabilities. CHASE departs from this single-classifier view: rather than thresholding scalar confidence, we turn rejection into a structured decision by explicitly comparing alternative explanations. Multi-hypothesis prediction: Modeling plausible answers stems from Multiple Choice Learning (Guzmán-Rivera et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017). Rupprecht et al. (2017) and probabilistic U-Nets (Kohl et al., 2018) cast multi-hypothesis heads as an explicit representation of ambiguity. However, they typically output multiple hypotheses without deciding between them. CHASE critically advances this by coupling hypothesis comparison with a separate, cost-aware ranking selector that explicitly learns an optimal abstention policy based on evidence strength. Temporal models and early-exit inference: Video tasks (Furnari and Farinella, 2021; Xu et al., 2019; Girdhar and Grauman, 2021; Wu et al., 2022) and early-exit networks (Teerapittayanon et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2018; Kaya et al., 2019; Ghodrati et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2019) face partial-observability and compute constraints. While a few inject epistemic uncertainty (Bao et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2022), most optimize for efficiency using standard softmax gates. They lack the ability to abstain based on conflicting structural evidence. CHASE fills this gap, demonstrating that sequential video inference under extreme ambiguity requires reasoning over explicit competing explanations.

2 Problem Setup and Evaluation Metrics

Selective prediction under ambiguity.

Given a sequence of d=6d=6 temporal descriptors 𝐱=(x1,…,xT)\mathbf{x}=(x_{1},\dots,x_{T}) extracted from a vesicle-pair video, the baseline task is to predict the underlying connectivity state y∈{connected,not_connected}y\in\{\text{connected},\text{not\_connected}\}. Because the connection evidence can be partially observable, some sequences do not support a reliable binary decision. In the simulator, these cases are marked by an ambiguity indicator a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, used only for evaluation and selector training. The model outputs a committed prediction y^\hat{y}, an accept score s⁡(𝐱)s(\mathbf{x}), and a final three-way decision y^final∈{connected,not_connected,abstain}\hat{y}_{\mathrm{final}}\in\{\text{connected},\text{not\_connected},\text{abstain}\}. Abstention is triggered when s⁡(𝐱)<τs(\mathbf{x})<\tau, where τ\tau is chosen on validation data to meet a target coverage c∈{0.80,0.90}c\in\{0.80,0.90\}.

Evaluation metrics.

A useful selective predictor should keep errors low among accepted sequences while assigning abstentions to genuinely ambiguous cases. We therefore report four metrics: (1) No-abstain accuracy, the binary accuracy when every sequence must be classified; (2) Risk@coverage, the error rate among accepted sequences at target coverage cc; (3) Three-way accuracy, where abstention is counted as correct only when a=1a=1; and (4) Abstain alignment, the fraction of abstentions that fall on sequences with a=1a=1. Together, these metrics distinguish low selective risk from ambiguity-aligned abstention (Figure 2 panel A).

3 Method

The pipeline (Figure 3) consists of three stages: (i) a hypothesis backbone scoring candidate classes; (ii) a seed ensemble and decision fusion capturing predictive disagreement; and (iii) a cost-aware pairwise selector outputting the final accept score. Crucially, the ground-truth ambiguity flag aa is never used to train the underlying classifiers; it enters only via a budgeted target during the selector’s validation-split training.

3.1 Stage 1: Hypothesis backbone

The backbone follows a simple intuition: the right class should be the one whose model of the world predicts the next frame more accurately. We instantiate two predictive heads - one for each class - and let them compete. A shared Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) (Cho et al., 2014) encodes context x1:T−1x_{1:T-1} into a hidden state hth_{t}. Two Gaussian heads (for c=connectedc=\text{connected} and n=not_connectedn=\text{not\_connected}) emit a mean and log-variance from hth_{t} to predict the next frame xt+1x_{t+1}. The frame-level negative log-likelihoods are time-averaged to yield per-class scores ℓc\ell^{c} and ℓn\ell^{n}. Simultaneously, an auxiliary head on pooled h1:T−1h_{1:T-1} outputs a softmax probability πaux\pi_{\mathrm{aux}}, which stabilizes training and provides a calibrated secondary signal for fusion and selector features. The backbone optimizes:

ℒbackbone=ℓy+λm​[m−(ℓy¯−ℓy)]++λc​CE​(πaux,y),\mathcal{L}_{\text{backbone}}\;=\;\ell^{y}\;+\;\lambda_{m}\big[m-(\ell^{\bar{y}}-\ell^{y})\big]_{+}\;+\;\lambda_{c}\mathrm{CE}(\pi^{\text{aux}},y), (1)

where y¯\bar{y} is the incorrect class, mm is a fixed margin, and [⋅]+=max⁡(0,⋅)[\,\cdot\,]_{+}=\max(0,\cdot). This forces the correct hypothesis to explain the data while maintaining a healthy margin between hypotheses-a critical gap we exploit to detect ambiguity. We extract the hypothesis-margin softmax πhyp=softmax⁡(−ℓc,−ℓn)\pi^{\text{hyp}}=\mathrm{softmax}(-\ell^{c},\,-\ell^{n}) and πaux\pi^{\text{aux}} for the selector.

3.2 Stage 2: Seed ensemble and decision fusion

To prevent fragility under stratified sampling, we train K=3K=3 backbones with different random seeds. Per-sequence outputs are averaged to obtain ensemble versions of πhyp\pi^{\text{hyp}}, πaux\pi^{\text{aux}}, and the score gap. The cross-seed dispersion-specifically, the standard deviations σhyp\sigma^{\text{hyp}} and σaux\sigma^{\text{aux}}, and the fraction of seeds disagreeing with the majority (δ\delta)-feed directly into the selector’s feature space. We fuse the probability sources via a scalar α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], tuned on the validation split: πfused=α​πhyp+(1−α)​πaux\pi^{\text{fused}}=\alpha\pi^{\text{hyp}}+(1-\alpha)\pi^{\text{aux}}. The committed prediction is y^=arg⁡max⁡πfused\hat{y}=\arg\max\pi^{\text{fused}}.

3.3 Stage 3: Cost-aware pairwise selector

We train a lightweight MLP fθf_{\theta} to map the ensemble-fused backbone summaries and dispersion signals ϕ⁡(𝐱)\phi(\mathbf{x}) to a scalar accept score. Training a selector on pure error E(𝐱)=𝟙[y^≠y]E(\mathbf{x})=\mathbb{1}[\hat{y}\neq y] provides noisy supervision on truly ambiguous sequences (essentially a coin flip), causing abstentions to be spent on the wrong examples. Instead, we train on a coverage-budgeted accept cost: ycost​(𝐱)=max⁡(E⁡(𝐱),γ⋅a)∈[0,1].y^{\text{cost}}(\mathbf{x})\;=\;\max\!\big(\,E(\mathbf{x}),\;\gamma\cdot a\,\big)\;\in\;[0,1]. Errors carry full cost, ambiguous-but-correct sequences carry cost γ\gamma, and ambiguous-and-wrong sequences carry full cost. The selector optimizes a binary cross-entropy (BCE) term alongside two pairwise ranking losses:

ℒsel=BCE⁡(fθ​(ϕ),ycost)+w⋅ℒrank​(E)+c⋅ℒrank​(ycost).\mathcal{L}_{\text{sel}}\;=\;\mathrm{BCE}\!\big(f_{\theta}(\phi),\,y^{\text{cost}}\big)\;+\;w\!\cdot\!\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}(E)\;+\;c\!\cdot\!\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}(y^{\text{cost}}). (2)

Here, ℒrank​(z)\mathcal{L}_{\text{rank}}(z) is a softplus margin loss applied to sequence pairs (i,j)(i,j) where zi>zjz_{i}>z_{j}, weighted by the difference zi−zjz_{i}-z_{j}. The EE-rank term explicitly pushes errors above correct commitments (optimizing risk@coverage), while the ycosty^{\text{cost}}-rank term gently lifts ambiguous sequences to fall below the threshold when budget allows. During inference, we compute the accept score s⁡(𝐱)=1−σ⁡(fθ​(ϕ))s(\mathbf{x})=1-\sigma(f_{\theta}(\phi)). A sequence is committed if s⁡(𝐱)≥τs(\mathbf{x})\geq\tau, where τ\tau meets the target empirical coverage cc on validation data.*

*The budgeted-cost weight γ=0.62\gamma=0.62 and pairwise weights w=0.66w=0.66, c=0.10c=0.10 were chosen by validation grid search to balance selective risk and abstain alignment (details in Appendix A).

4 Physically Grounded Simulator and Real Data

4.1 GUV-Inspired Simulator Design

We developed a targeted 2D kinematic simulator to systematically stress-test selective inference. The vesicles move in a unit box under Brownian motion, optional shared drift, and-for connected pairs-spring coupling that keeps them physically linked. As illustrated in Figure 2 panel B, the simulator generates 64-frame sequences (approx. 6 seconds) of vesicle pairs under two latent states: connected and not connected.

Latent activity profiles and matched pairs.

To ensure classifiers rely on temporal reasoning rather than simple global summaries, the simulator uses latent activity profiles u⁡(t)∈[0,1]u(t)\in[0,1] that control when evidence becomes visible. For connected sequences, u⁡(t)u(t) modulates the strength of the spring coupling or the visibility of the visual "bridge" (representing the physical membrane neck). For matched negative sequences, the identical u⁡(t)u(t) timing is reused, but instead of physical coupling, it triggers shared fluid drift and temporary proximity. This creates matched pairs with similar global summary statistics but different causal mechanisms. We focus on two challenging regimes (Figure 2 panel B): (1) Intermittent coupling: Dynamic spring linkage is matched with a negative sequence exhibiting coordinated shared drift. (2) Short local evidence: A brief window of strong coupling is matched with a brief motion distractor. These pairings force the model to distinguish true physical linkage from coincidental proximity.

Features, ambiguity, and dataset splits.

For each frame, we extract six continuous features that form the input vector 𝐱\mathbf{x} (as defined in Section 2): Euclidean distance (between vesicle centroids), distance change (frame-to-frame), relative motion (alignment of velocity vectors), spatial support count (bridge region pixel area), median bridge score (visual intensity/confidence), and median bridge width. Sequences are assigned an ambiguity level α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1], which scales observation noise and degrades visual bridge evidence. Sequences with α≥0.75\alpha\geq 0.75 are explicitly flagged as truly_ambiguous (a=1a=1) and constitute the very-high (VH) ambiguity subset, which we contrast against the overall dataset (full test set).

4.2 Qualitative Zero-Shot Transfer to Real GUV Data

Real phase-separated GUVs were prepared via electroformation, subjected to hypertonic stress, and imaged using spinning-disc confocal fluorescence microscopy (details in Appendix B). For the selected qualitative examples, connectivity was assessed using 3D reconstruction. However, 3D confocal imaging can establish whether vesicles are attached, but does not always resolve the fine neck structure itself, since the optical resolution is much larger than the lipid membrane thickness. Thus, the available real videos are suitable for qualitative physical grounding, but not for a comprehensive quantitative benchmark across all ambiguity regimes.

Because 2D projections of 3D physical processes natively produce misleading visual evidence-where real connections may feature invisible tethers, and disconnected pairs may exhibit correlated motion due to fluid drift-this empirical data perfectly encapsulates the partial observability problem. Without any retraining or threshold adjustments, we extract the identical six features from the real sequences using Cellpose (Stringer et al., 2021) and active boundary tracking. We apply the simulator-trained CHASE model strictly zero-shot to these sequences to illustrate whether the model behaves conservatively when real-world visual evidence is incomplete or potentially misleading.

5 Experiments

5.1 Experimental Setup

The full simulated dataset comprises 3,360 total sequences, generated by creating matched pairs across the two regimes to yield 2,400 training, 480 validation, and 480 test sequences. We use 5-fold cross-validation stratified by label, subtype, and ambiguity bin. In each fold, 20% of sequences are held out for testing and 20% of validation split within each training fold is used to train the selector, tune hyperparameters, and determine the coverage threshold τ\tau. Hyperparameters remain fixed across all folds and coverages. We compare CHASE against a standard single-branch Maximum Softmax Probability (MSP) baseline, alongside canonical methods from two families: epistemic uncertainty estimation-MC Dropout (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016) and Deep Ensembles (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017), and learned selective classification-SelectiveNet (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019), Deep Gamblers (Liu et al., 2019), and ConfidNet (Corbière et al., 2019). We omit multi-hypothesis models and temporal early-exit networks here, as they either lack native selective abstention or are primarily optimized for compute efficiency rather than ambiguity-awareness. For rigorous comparison, all external baselines utilize the identical precomputed 6-feature input and adapt to the GRU backbone, isolating performance differences strictly to their uncertainty and abstention mechanisms. We report means and standard deviations across the five test folds. All experiments were run on a single NVIDIA RTX A5000 GPU. Across five folds, CHASE trained in 30.68±0.3530.68\pm 0.35 s per fold, and scored test set in 1.46±0.051.46\pm 0.05 s, corresponding to 2.17±0.082.17\pm 0.08 ms per sequence. Significance (p<0.05p<0.05) is assessed using a one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test across the folds.

5.2 Main Quantitative Results: Simulated Benchmark

Table 1 presents the full quantitative comparison across all ambiguity regimes and the very-high ambiguity subset on our simulated dataset. Traditional uncertainty baselines (e.g., Deep Ensembles and MC Dropout) often achieve low risk by conservatively discarding difficult sequences. In contrast, CHASE is optimized for ambiguity-aware abstention, yielding its strongest gains in ambiguity-oriented metrics. For three-way accuracy, CHASE achieves statistically significant improvements (p<0.05p<0.05) over the respective strongest baselines on both the overall dataset (+4.3% relative gain at 80% coverage; +3.2% at 90%) and the VH ambiguity subset (+6.5% at 80%; +8.8% at 90%). For overall abstain alignment, CHASE drives a statistically significant improvement at 80% coverage (+6.3% relative gain) alongside substantial mean improvements at 90% coverage (+11.0%), while all methods naturally hit 100% alignment in the severely degraded VH regime. Crucially, these ambiguity-awareness gains do not compromise standard classification: CHASE achieves statistically significant gains in overall no-abstain accuracy (91.01%) while maintaining the highest mean performance on the VH subset (86.99%). Finally, CHASE successfully safeguards standard selective risk; it performs at par with the top baselines at 80% coverage (tying MC Dropout at 3.87% overall risk), and substantially improves over the respective strongest baselines at the 90% coverage target, yielding relative risk reductions of 9.9% overall and 4.4% on the VH subset.

5.3 Ablation Study

To isolate architectural contributions, we evaluate CHASE variants in Table 2. We first establish the necessity of the dual-hypothesis backbone: models restricted to a single hypothesis fail entirely ( 50% no-abstain accuracy). Conversely, explicitly comparing two hypotheses (Dual Hypothesis + MSP) drops baseline risk compared to a Single-Branch GRU, confirming that structural comparison is inherently more informative. Next, we evaluate the selector mechanisms. An ordinary selector trained solely on binary error achieves the lowest absolute risk but indiscriminately rejects sequences, stagnating three-way accuracy and alignment. Introducing the budgeted ambiguity cost corrects this, aligning abstentions with true structural uncertainty and causing three-way accuracy to surge. Fusing the auxiliary score further peaks overall three-way accuracy (75.36% at 80% coverage, 72.53 at 90% coverage) and abstain alignment (61.30% at 80%, 67.60 at 90%).

To resolve the resulting regression in selective risk (which rises to 4.50%), we apply our final stabilization components: 3-seed ensembling and the pairwise ranking margin. The final CHASE configuration deliberately trades a slight reduction in overall three-way accuracy (settling at 71.85% and 71.04% for the 80% and 90% coverage targets, respectively) in order to strictly recover the baseline risk boundary. Specifically, it reduces the overall risk to 3.87% and 5.72%, performing at or above the strongest baselines in Table 1, while simultaneously achieving the lowest risk in all ablated components on the VH ambiguity subset in both coverages. This conscious compromise ensures the model safely guards stringent risk requirements while maximizing no-abstain accuracy and maintaining perfect 100% abstain alignment on the VH ambiguity subset.

5.4 Qualitative Zero-Shot Transfer to Real GUV Videos

We evaluate the simulator-trained CHASE model on real GUV sequences zero-shot. As Figure 4 demonstrates, while the no-abstain prediction branch correctly identifies the underlying physical tendency (connected vs. disconnected), the final selector safely abstains across all three evaluated cases: missing 2D observability, a hidden structural neck, and visual nesting. This is the exact intended behavior. 2D microscopy natively suffers from partial observability: true 3D connections may exist out-of-planes, and visually nested disconnected pairs often exhibit misleading correlated motion due to shared fluid drift. CHASE successfully decouples these signals-capturing the likely physical state while safely withholding commitment when 2D visual evidence is insufficient to guarantee structural certainty.

6 Discussion and Limitations

Our results demonstrate that ambiguity-aware selective prediction requires explicitly comparing competing hypotheses to reliably identify contradictory evidence. However, we note two primary limitations. First, while CHASE achieves strong mean improvements across all metrics, its most robust, statistically significant gains are concentrated in three-way accuracy, abstain alignment (at 80% coverage), and no-abstain accuracy. Because improvements in absolute selective risk and higher-coverage abstain alignment exhibit cross-fold variance, CHASE’s core advantage lies in recognizing structural ambiguity rather than drastically pushing the selective risk boundary. Second, our quantitative evaluation relies on a physically motivated simulator. Although rigorously controlled for realistic failure modes (e.g., shared fluid drift and hidden necks), our empirical GUV dataset lacks the scale and comprehensive ground truth required for quantitative testing. While CHASE successfully navigated real-world artifacts in zero-shot transfer, future work must scale to large, fully annotated empirical datasets to completely validate cross-domain robustness.

7 Broader Impact

In biophysics and medical imaging, forced AI predictions on misleading evidence can invalidate downstream analyses. CHASE mitigates this by safely automating clear cases while explicitly flagging ambiguous sequences for expert review. Accurately resolving GUV connectivity illuminates fundamental membrane dynamics (e.g., cell fusion, fission, and communication), directly advancing synthetic cell design and targeted drug/mRNA delivery. However, a potential risk is over-reliance on abstention as an absolute safety guarantee. In real scientific workflows, CHASE must function strictly as a triage tool rather than an autonomous source of physical ground truth.

8 Conclusion

We introduced CHASE, a selective prediction framework that evaluates competing temporal hypotheses-advancing beyond standard confidence thresholds, ensemble variance, and uncoupled multi-hypothesis outputs-to safely navigate structured ambiguity. On a physically grounded benchmark, CHASE maintained the highest no-abstain accuracy and performed at-par in selective risk against canonical baselines. Crucially, CHASE delivered statistically significant gains over the respective strongest baselines in overall no-abstain accuracy, three-way accuracy, and overall abstain alignment (at 80% coverage). Furthermore, it yielded up to an 11.0% relative mean improvement in overall alignment and a 9.9% relative reduction in overall selective risk at the stricter 90% coverage target. Qualitative zero-shot transfer to empirical GUV videos further demonstrates CHASE as a principled solution for safe selective inference when partial observability renders forced binary classification unsafe.

Appendix A Appendix: Hyperparameter Sweep and Sensitivity Analysis

To configure the final CHASE architecture, we conducted a localized hyperparameter sweep adjusting the weights assigned to the components of the selector loss function: the pairwise ranking margin (gg, representing the budgeted cost γ\gamma), the wrong-prediction cost (ww), and the budgeted ambiguity cost (cc). The table below presents the detailed performance metrics across these configurations at both coverage levels. The chosen balance (γ=0.62,w=0.66,c=0.10\gamma=0.62,w=0.66,c=0.10) is highlighted. This specific configuration for γ=0.62\gamma=0.62 was chosen because it optimally stabilizes standard classification risk while fiercely protecting abstain alignment on ambiguous cases, avoiding the severe performance drops seen when over-optimizing for a single objective.

Training and Architecture Details.

The backbone uses a single-layer GRU (hidden size 64) and a two-layer MLP auxiliary head, trained for 30 epochs (batch size 64, patience 6) with margin m=1.0m=1.0, λm=1.0\lambda_{m}=1.0, and auxiliary weight λc=1.5\lambda_{c}=1.5. The seed ensemble uses K=3K=3 members (seeds {42,143,244}\{42,143,244\}). The decision fusion scalar α\alpha is tuned via grid search over 21 evenly spaced points on [0,1][0,1]. The selector is a two-layer MLP (width 24, dropout 0.1), trained for up to 80 epochs (patience 8).

Reproducibility.

We will publicly release code for simulator generation, model training, baseline evaluation, and table reproduction after acceptance. Real GUV videos are used only for qualitative illustration; if raw videos cannot be released, we will provide the extracted feature sequences used for Figure 4, subject to institutional data-sharing constraints.

Appendix B Real GUV Data

Preparation of GUVs

The phase separated GUVs are prepared using standard electroformation technique, composed of 38 mol% 1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3phosphocholine (DOPC), 38 mol% 1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DPPC) and 20 mol% Cholesterol (Ch). To enable visualization of the membrane by fluorescence microscopy, the GUVs are doped with 1 mol% 1,2- dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3phosphoethanolamine-N-(lissamine rhodamine B sulfonyl) (Rho-DOPE), and 3 mol% 1,2-diphytanoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine-N-(7-nitro-2-1,3-benzoxadiazol-4-yl) (ammonium salt) (NBD-DPPE). Rho-DOPE prefers distributing in Ld phase and NBD-DPPE distributes more in Lo phase, enabling phase identification and GUV imaging. When preparing GUVs, the lipids are dissolved in chloroform at 2 mM total concentration. 20 μ\muL lipid solution was deposited on to a clean ITO glass slides and desiccated overnight. An O-ring entrapping 240 μ\muL 100 mM sucrose solution that hydrated the lipids during GUV formation was sandwiched between two ITO slides, sealed with vacuum grease. When conducting electroformation, the sandwich was subjected to 1 hour of alternating electric field (10 Hz, 1.1 V) at 60∘C, after which the sample was held at 50∘C, 40∘C and 30∘C for 20 minutes each, progressively to obtain 5-50 μ\mum sized GUVs.

Deformation of GUVs

5 μ\muL of the prepared GUV suspension containing 100 mM sucrose was subjected 45 μ\muL of 100 mM glucose bath in a 96-well plate. To apply the hypertonic stress, 12.5 μ\muL of 300 mM glucose solution was injected into the same well via a syringe pump at flow rate of 12.5 μ\muL/min. The final concentration of the bath in well is 140 mM.

Time-lapse imaging

The time-lapse images of the GUVs under hypertonic stress were carried out on a Nikon Ti2-E inverted microscope, which is equipped with a spinning disc confocal (SDC) - confocal spinning unit (CSU)(GATACA SYSTEMS). Excitation was provided by a 488 nm and 561 nm laser to excite NBD-DPPE (fluoresces green) and Rho-DOPE (fluoresces red), respectively. Fluorescence images were acquired using a 100X/1.45 Plan-Apo oil-immersion objective, and captured by dual Orca Fusion sCMOS cameras (Hamamatsu). Time-lapse images acquisition was controlled by MetaMorph (Molecular Device) software at time interval of 1 s.
